primary_claim: A logistic-regression probe trained on token-level falsehood labels precisely highlights the specific tokens that make a statement false, working well on a small toy Q&A dataset with Qwen2.5-0.5B and outperforming mean-activation and last-token baseline probes, even at statement-level classification.

effect.metric: qualitative comparison of token-level probe vs. mean/last-token baseline probes on held-out samples

stated_future_work: iterate on training data to test out-of-distribution generalization more thoroughly
go on-policy and aim to detect a model's 'intent to lie' rather than generic falsehood
check whether a linearly-probable 'current word is false' direction also holds for safety-relevant properties like an inserted code bug
implement stronger baselines such as attention-based probes or max-score probes
run an ablation offsetting all labels by one token to test whether the probe can learn pretty much anything
limitations_stated: the probe doesn't immediately generalize out of distribution in a quick test
probes are trained off-policy on Claude-written text rather than text the studied model (Qwen) would have produced, so they cannot detect 'intention to lie' or lies only clear from future tokens
small dataset: ~500 Q&A samples total, only ~100 with per-token labels
the test set was reused as a validation set to pick the regularization coefficient instead of using a separate validation set
only the usual baselines (mean activation, last token) were implemented, not stronger baselines like attention-based probes
quote: The new method works very well, exactly as intended. The incorrect tokens are highlighted, and nothing else is.
